questions.question: Which statement best captures PostgreSQL's durability boundary?
options: A transaction is durable when every changed heap page is written immediately
A transaction can be acknowledged after its required WAL record is durable, even if data pages are written later
A transaction is durable when a read replica applies it
A transaction is durable when autovacuum observes it
questions.explanation: Write-ahead logging records changes before dirty data pages. Crash recovery replays durable WAL, so the acknowledgement policy is tied to WAL durability rather than immediate heap-page writes.

questions.question: Why can raising work_mem from 8 MB to 128 MB create an outage even when one test query becomes faster?
options: work_mem is allocated exactly once for the whole server
work_mem disables the operating-system page cache
Several active sorts or hashes in many concurrent plans may each allocate up to the configured amount
work_mem permanently expands every table
questions.explanation: work_mem is a per-operation budget. Concurrent plans can contain multiple memory-consuming operators, so pool width, plan shape, and workload concurrency determine the real envelope.

questions.question: What does MVCC primarily allow PostgreSQL to do?
options: Serve readers from visible row versions while writers create newer versions
Skip transaction IDs for read-only statements
Store every index entirely in memory
Guarantee that replicas never lag
questions.explanation: MVCC lets each transaction evaluate row-version visibility from its snapshot. Readers usually do not block writers, but obsolete versions must later be reclaimed.

questions.question: A Read Committed transaction runs two related SELECT statements while another transaction commits between them. What can happen?
options: Both statements must use the same snapshot
The second statement can see a newer committed state than the first
The first statement automatically locks every row it reads
PostgreSQL always aborts the reader
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL Read Committed takes a new snapshot for each statement. Use Repeatable Read for a stable transaction snapshot when a multi-query report must describe one point in time.

questions.question: What must an application do when a Serializable PostgreSQL transaction fails with a serialization error?
options: Retry only the final SQL statement against the old snapshot
Ignore the error because PostgreSQL committed the transaction
Retry the complete transaction with a fresh snapshot and bounded backoff
Disable WAL for the retry
questions.explanation: Serializable Snapshot Isolation preserves correctness by aborting dangerous dependency structures. The whole unit of work must be recomputed in a new transaction.

questions.question: Which index is the normal first choice for equality lookups, ordered ranges, and ORDER BY on scalar columns?
options: B-tree
GIN
GiST
BRIN
questions.explanation: B-tree is PostgreSQL's general-purpose ordered index. GIN suits multi-valued containment, GiST supports extensible geometric and range strategies, and BRIN summarizes naturally ordered large tables.

questions.question: Why can a long-running transaction increase storage and query pressure?
options: It forces every new connection to use Serializable isolation
Its old snapshot can prevent vacuum from reclaiming row versions that may still be visible to it
It converts all indexes into hash indexes
It disables checkpoints permanently
questions.explanation: Vacuum cannot remove a version that an active snapshot may still need. Long transactions therefore retain dead tuples, increase bloat, and can delay transaction-ID cleanup.

questions.question: A replica is promoted after the primary fails. Which condition matters most for correctness?
options: The replica has the largest shared_buffers setting
Clients are fenced from the old primary and the promoted node has replayed the required WAL
Autovacuum is disabled during promotion
Every read query uses an unlogged table
questions.explanation: Failover needs both state and authority: the promoted node must have the required WAL, and the old writer must be fenced so two primaries cannot accept conflicting writes.
